prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

While that my soul repairs to her devotion, Here I intomb my flesh, that it betimes May take acquaintance of this heap of dust; To which the blast of death's incessant motion, Fed with the exhalation of our crimes, Drives all at last. Therefore I gladly trustMy body to this school, that it may learn To spell his elements, and find his birth Written in dusty heraldry and lines ; Which dissolution sure doth best discern, Comparing dust with dust, and earth with earth. These laugh at jet, and marble put for signs,To sever the good fellowship of dust, And spoil the meeting. What shall point out them, When they shall bow, and kneel, and fall down flat To kiss those heaps, which now they have in trust? Dear flesh, while I do pray, learn here thy stem And true descent: that when thou shalt grow fat,And wanton in thy cravings, thou mayst know, That flesh is but the glass, which holds the dust That measures all our time; which also shall Be crumbled into dust. Mark, here below, How tame these ashes are, how free from lust, That thou mayst fit thyself against thy fall.

outputs.L1:
While my soul repairs to her devotion,  
Here I entomb my flesh, that it betimes  
May make acquaintance with this heap of dust,  
To which the blast of death’s incessant motion,  
Fed by the exhalation of our crimes,  
Drives all at last. Therefore, I gladly entrust  
My body to this school, that it may learn  
To spell its elements and find its birth  
Written in dusty heraldry and lines—  
Truths dissolution surely best discerns  
By comparing dust with dust and earth with earth.  
These laugh at jet and marble set as signs  
To sever the good fellowship of dust  
And spoil the meeting. What shall distinguish them  
When they bow, kneel, and fall down flat  
To kiss those heaps they now hold in trust?  
Dear flesh, while I pray, learn here thy stem  
And true descent, so that when thou growest fat  
And wanton in thy cravings, thou mayst know  
That flesh is but the glass that holds the dust  
Which measures all our time—and which shall also  
Be crumbled into dust. Mark here below  
How tame these ashes are, how free from lust,  
That thou mayst prepare thyself against thy fall.
outputs.L2:
While my spirit turns to prayer, I lay my body here as though in a tomb, so that it may begin early to understand this mound of earth—the final place toward which death’s relentless force, strengthened by the vapors of human sin, eventually carries everyone. I willingly entrust my body to this place of instruction, where it can study the substance from which it came and recognize its ancestry in the dusty inscriptions and emblems of the dead. Decay teaches this truth most clearly by setting dust beside dust and earth beside earth.

These remains mock the black stone and marble monuments erected to distinguish one person’s dust from another and to break apart their common fellowship. How will such markers identify them when the monuments themselves bend, sink, and collapse, falling upon the very heaps they were meant to guard?

Beloved body, while I pray, study your origin and your true lineage. Then, when you grow prosperous and indulge your appetites, remember that the flesh is only an hourglass containing the dust by which our lives are measured—and that the glass itself will also crumble into dust. Observe how quiet and submissive these ashes are, entirely released from desire, and prepare yourself accordingly for your own inevitable fall.
outputs.L3:
While the speaker’s body remains among the tombs, contemplating the reality of mortality, his soul turns toward prayer. In this setting, death appears as the consequence of human sin and as the great equalizer that ultimately reduces every person, regardless of status or wealth, to dust. The grave thus becomes a kind of school: it teaches the body both its earthly origin and its inevitable return to the earth.

The monuments surrounding the dead may be fashioned from costly materials such as jet and marble, but their splendor cannot preserve lasting distinctions between individuals. Beneath these ornate memorials, the remains of the dead mingle together, making social rank and worldly identity meaningless. Reflecting on these humble ashes—now free from ambition, appetite, and desire—the speaker addresses his own flesh. He urges it to restrain its cravings, learn from the dead, and prepare itself for the same unavoidable end.
